articles.title: What does “verified” mean for a company-research agent?
articles.excerpt: Disclosure: I’m Soham, founder of Builderr. We’re running Signalpost, a challenge for agents that research Norwegian companies. I want to share the design question behind it, because it’s easy to miss…
articles.body: Disclosure: I’m Soham, founder of Builderr. We’re running Signalpost, a challenge for agents that research Norwegian companies. I want to share the design question behind it, because it’s easy to miss when a result looks polished. A company-research agent can return a real fact, cite a real page, and still be wrong if that page belongs to a parent company or a similarly named business. A useful profile needs to get the entity right before it gathers facts. It also needs to show where each fact came from, when it was checked, and what it could not verify. In Signalpost, the agent receives a Norwegian company number and must return a complete profile from public information. The challenge scores coverage, fact accuracy and evidence, synthesis, and ease of checking.

articles.title: Check your landing page at 320px wide before you ship
articles.excerpt: Most landing page checks happen on a wide desktop window and one phone. There is a cheap check in between that catches a lot: look at the page at 320 CSS pixels wide and see whether you have to scroll…
articles.body: Most landing page checks happen on a wide desktop window and one phone. There is a cheap check in between that catches a lot: look at the page at 320 CSS pixels wide and see whether you have to scroll sideways to read it. This is WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.10 (Reflow). It says content should work without two-dimensional scrolling at a width equivalent to 320 CSS pixels. W3C notes that 320 CSS pixels is what a 1280px wide window looks like at 400% zoom, so it is also what a low-vision user on a laptop can end up with. The check Open DevTools and set the viewport to 320px wide (or set the browser to 400% zoom on a 1280px window). Scroll the whole page from top to bottom. If you can scroll sideways, or text is cut off, something is too wide.
articles.author: Kai Mercer

articles.title: Graphic Guide: Stop Staring at Spreadsheets: Analyze Data with ChatGPT
articles.excerpt: A sales spreadsheet can contain hundreds of numbers and still leave a team unsure what to do next. How can ChatGPT help turn a table into useful analysis—and how can the team check that a plausible ex…
articles.body: A sales spreadsheet can contain hundreds of numbers and still leave a team unsure what to do next. How can ChatGPT help turn a table into useful analysis—and how can the team check that a plausible explanation is supported by evidence? This comic follows a team working with fictional monthly sales data. They define the decision they need to support, inspect column names, units, and blanks, then use ChatGPT to calculate changes, visualize trends, and explore possible explanations. Along the way, they check formulas and source records and keep confirmed facts separate from hypotheses and next steps. The team checks a blank against the fictional source note instead of treating it as zero, verifies a percentage formula and chart, and notices that a rising total can hide a fall in store sales.

articles.title: Regression-testing an Excel/VBA report with golden files
articles.excerpt: The VBA that a business depends on is rarely a library. Usually it's one macro that reads a few files, builds a report and saves it. You can unit-test that (Rubberduck has a unit-testing framework for…
articles.body: The VBA that a business depends on is rarely a library. Usually it's one macro that reads a few files, builds a report and saves it. You can unit-test that (Rubberduck has a unit-testing framework for VBA), but the client's question is simpler: is the report the same as yesterday, apart from what I asked you to change? A golden file answers exactly that. The idea Run the macro once on known input and check the output by hand. Once it's right, approve it and keep it as the golden file. After each change, run the macro on the same input and compare the new output with the golden, cell by cell. Every difference is a bug or a change you meant to make. If you meant it, approve the new output on purpose. Don't let anything overwrite the golden quietly.

articles.body: Using the NASA X-ray spacecraft Swift combined with radio observations, astronomers have observed a supermassive black hole burping radio jets 300 days after a heavy cosmic meal. The team was also able to roughly estimate the mass of this feeding cosmic titan, which sits at the heart of the Perseus Cluster, a massive collection of thousands of galaxies. The black hole sits at the center of the galaxy NGC 1275, located around 225 light-years away, and is the brightest galaxy of the Perseus Cluster . The supermassive black hole first flared in X-rays, which indicated an increase in the rate at which it was accreting matter.

The agency opened a "Lunar Grounding Challenge" to avoid situations where an astronaut on the moon could become "a walking, high voltage capacitor." Submissions for the $150,000 competition are due Jan. 15 and you can see the requirements here . NASA is hoping to put astronaut boots at the lunar south pole in 2028 during the Artemis 4 or 5 missions, on the first landing mission since NASA's Apollo 17 in 1972. But simulations suggest that both "tribocharging" (electric-charge transfer between two objects) and plasma charging (from ambient gas in the region) could build up electric charge on spacesuits.

articles.title: The 'Halloween Fireballs' are coming. Here's what to expect from the Taurids this year
articles.excerpt: The Southern and Northern Taurid meteor showers will produce occasional bright, slow-moving meteors worldwide during October and November, with moon-free peaks in 2026.
articles.body: They don't produce anything like the torrent of "shooting stars" associated with August's Perseids or December's Geminids, but the Taurid meteor showers have something else going for them — fireballs. The Taurids are famous for occasionally producing exceptionally bright, slow-moving meteors that can streak dramatically across the night sky from September to December. As a bonus, they're visible from both the Northern and Southern hemispheres. That's because they appear to emanate from the constellation Taurus, which sits close to the ecliptic, the apparent path the sun takes across the sky as Earth orbits around it. The Taurids are actually two closely related showers — the Southern Taurids and Northern Taurids — whose activity overlaps in late October and November.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 12, 1964: The Soviet Union launches Voskhod 1, the 1st multi-person cosmonaut crew, into space
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 12, 1964, the Soviet Union launched Voskhod 1, a 24-hour crewed mission that achieved several "firsts" for human spaceflight. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 12, 1964, the Soviet Union launched Voskhod 1, a 24-hour crewed mission that achieved several "firsts" for human spaceflight . This was the first time that a spacecraft carried more than one person into orbit, with three cosmonauts packed inside the spacecraft. Only two cosmonauts were originally supposed to fly on this mission, but Soviet politicians pressured the Russian space program to add one more. This left no room for spacesuits on board, so this also became the first spaceflight without spacesuits . Two of the crewmembers, an engineer and a doctor, became the first civilians to go to space. On Oct. 12, 1964, the Soviet Union launched the first multiperson mission, Voskhod 1, which launched three Russian cosmonauts into space.

articles.title: Namibian salt flats look like an alien planet | Space photo of the day for Oct. 12, 2026
articles.excerpt: The Etosha Pan in northern Namibia, the largest salt flat in the country, looks otherworldly in this satellite photo.
articles.body: The Etosha Pan, Namibia's largest salt pan, seen from space. (Image credit: Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data (2026), processed by ESA) A neon blue pool swirls amongst what look like clouds, all surrounded by a bright red stretch of land. This might look like the surface of an alien planet , but it's actually a salt flat right here on Earth , seen from space. What is it? Etosha National Park in northern Namibia hosts the largest salt pan, or piece of land covered with salt and other minerals, in the country. This image of the Etosha Pan was captured on April 5 of this year by Europe's Copernicus Sentinel-2 mission, which consists of two identical satellites in the same orbit.

articles.title: How the impossible geometry of 'Tomb Raider III''s UFO level was made
articles.excerpt: Bigger on the inside? Where have we heard that before?
articles.body: "Tomb Raider" celebrates its 30th anniversary this month. While many remember the iconic T-Rex or locking Winston the Butler in the freezer, many forget about the UFO in 1998’s "Tomb Raider III"; a mysterious alien craft that worked a lot like Doctor Who ’s TARDIS. Coming off the back of the hugely successful "Tomb Raider 2", developer Core Design had big plans for the third entry, including kayaking, those iconic London levels, and, of course, a level featuring a UFO in Area 51. Although it looked small on the outside, the UFO featured multiple floors for players to explore as they searched for a vital artifact, all as enemies swarmed in.
